forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

findings.paper_title: AR Appendix 1 - Unaudited Draft Statement of Accounts 2025-26 Pension Fund
findings.headline: Triennial actuarial valuation completed March 2026 with revised contribution rates in effect from 1 April 2026
findings.detail: The fund's triennial actuarial valuation as at 31 March 2025 was completed in March 2026. This valuation determines revised employer contribution rates effective from 1 April 2026. The prior valuation (March 2022) had set a primary rate of 17.2% of pensionable pay and secondary (deficit recovery) contributions averaging £16.9m per annum for 2023-26 over a 14.7-year recovery period. The new rates are not disclosed in this document.
findings.matters: New pension contribution rates represent a material fixed-cost pressure on council finances; rates typically rise following valuations and are set by actuarial assumptions beyond the council's control.
findings.figures: Prior primary rate 17.2%; prior secondary rate £16.9m per annum (2023-26); prior deficit recovery period 14.7 years; deficit at March 2022 valuation £245m
findings.quote: The triennial actuarial valuation as at 31 March 2025 was completed March 2026. Based on the results of this valuation, the contribution rates payable by the individual employers will be revised with effect from 1 April 2026.

findings.paper_title: AR Appendix 1 - Unaudited Draft Statement of Accounts 2025-26 Pension Fund
findings.headline: Lump sum payments to pension scheme leavers increased 4-fold to £11.0m
findings.detail: Payments to and on account of leavers (primarily refunds of member contributions and transfer values) increased sharply from £2.8m in 2024-25 to £11.0m in 2025-26. This 4-fold increase represents material cash outflow relative to annual contributions and may reflect changes in scheme utilisation or membership.
findings.matters: Unexpected spikes in pension benefit outflows create cash flow volatility; understanding whether this is structural or temporary affects the fund's long-term contribution forecasts.
findings.figures: 2025-26 payments to leavers £11.0m; 2024-25 payments £2.8m; increase of £8.2m (290%)
findings.quote: Payments to and on Account of Leavers 11,001 [£'000 in 2025/26]

findings.paper_title: AR Appendix 1 - Unaudited Draft Statement of Accounts 2025-26 Pension Fund
findings.headline: Employer and employee contributions declined 4.8% to £68.2m in 2025-26
findings.detail: Contributions receivable fell from £71.7m to £68.2m year-on-year. The decline occurred across the financial year as the council and its scheme employers reduced contributions. This warrants monitoring to establish whether it reflects structural changes in workforce size or pay, or temporary factors.
findings.matters: A material decline in pension contribution income could signal workforce contraction or pay pressures that also constrain council borrowing and service delivery capacity.

findings.paper_title: AR Appendix 1 - Unaudited Draft Statement of Accounts 2025-26 Pension Fund
findings.headline: Pension fund deficit reduced to £207m with IAS 19 funding ratio improving to 84.3%
findings.detail: The fund's funding ratio on an IAS 19 basis improved from 82.8% to 84.3% year-on-year, reducing the deficit from £223m to £207m. This improvement occurred despite employer and employee contributions declining 4.8% to £68.2m, indicating the fund benefited from strong investment returns. The fund's solvency funding level had improved from 80% in 2019 to 81% at the 2022 valuation.
findings.matters: A pension fund in improving financial health reduces the risk of unsustainable contribution demands damaging a council's borrowing capacity and service finances.
findings.figures: Net assets £1,114.2m vs liabilities £1,321m (2025-26); net assets £1,079.5m vs liabilities £1,303m (2024-25); contributions £68.2m (2025-26) vs £71.7m (2024-25)
findings.quote: The estimated net present value of pension fund assets and liabilities on an IAS 19 basis is as follows: [Net present value of liabilities] (1,321,000) [Net assets] 1,114,218 [£'000]

findings.paper_title: AR Appendix 3 - LBWFPF- 31 March 2022 FSS - Final
findings.headline: Climate scenario modeling shows funding impacts of 15% after 20 years and 29% after 40 years in failed transition scenario
findings.detail: The fund has modeled three climate scenarios showing potential funding impacts. Near-term impacts (5 years) range from 2-4% negative under orderly or rapid transition paths. Worst-case failed transition scenario shows cumulative impacts of 15% after 20 years and 29% after 40 years due to physical climate risks. Actuary concludes current prudence in assumptions is adequate but notes climate-related impacts could materially stress the funding plan, particularly when combined with other risks.
findings.matters: Forward-looking climate risk analysis identifies potential material funding pressures that could affect contribution requirements in future valuations. Fund's systematic monitoring supports proactive risk management.
findings.figures: 4% (Rapid Transition, 5 years); 2% after 5 years, 4% after 20 years, 10% after 40 years (Orderly Transition); 15% after 20 years and 29% after 40 years (Failed Transition)
findings.quote: However, any climate related impacts will potentially put significant stress on the funding plan, especially when taken into account with other risk factors so needs to be monitored over time.
